<p dir="auto">Redis provides a variety of data types, processing engines, and capabilities to support a wide range of use cases:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings" rel="nofollow">
<strong>String:</strong>
</a>
 Sequences of bytes, including text, serialized objects, and binary arrays used for caching, counters, and bitwise operations.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/json/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>JSON:</strong>
</a>
 Nested JSON documents that are indexed and searchable using JSONPath expressions and with 
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/" rel="nofollow">Redis Search</a>
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/arrays/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Array:</strong>
</a>
 Sparse, index-addressable collection of string values
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Hash:</strong>
</a>
 Field-value maps used to represent basic objects and store groupings of key-value pairs with support for 
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/#field-expiration" rel="nofollow">hash field expiration (TTL)</a>
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Redis Search:</strong>
</a>
 Use Redis as a document database, a vector database, a secondary index, and a search engine. Define indexes for hash and JSON documents and then use a rich query language for vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, and aggregations.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/lists/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>List:</strong>
</a>
 Linked lists of string values used as stacks, queues, and for queue management.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sets/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Set:</strong>
</a>
 Unordered collection of unique strings used for tracking unique items, relations, and common set operations (intersections, unions, differences).
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Sorted set:</strong>
</a>
 Collection of unique strings ordered by an associated score used for leaderboards and rate limiters.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/vector-sets/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Vector set (beta):</strong>
</a>
 Collection of vector embeddings used for semantic similarity search, semantic caching, semantic routing, and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Geospatial indexes:</strong>
</a>
 Coordinates used for finding nearby points within a given radius or bounding box.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitmaps/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Bitmap:</strong>
</a>
 A set of bit-oriented operations defined on the string type used for efficient set representations and object permissions.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitfields/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Bitfield:</strong>
</a>
 Binary-encoded strings that let you set, increment, and get integer values of arbitrary bit length used for limited-range counters, numeric values, and multi-level object permissions such as role-based access control (RBAC)
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/hyperloglogs/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Hyperloglog:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure for approximating the cardinality of a set used for analytics such as counting unique visits, form fills, etc.
</li>
<li>
*
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/bloom-filter/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Bloom filter:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure to check if a given value is present in a set. Used for fraud detection, ad placement, and unique column (i.e. username/email/slug) checks.
</li>
<li>
*
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/cuckoo-filter/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Cuckoo filter:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure for checking if a given value is present in a set while also allowing limited counting and deletions used in targeted advertising and coupon code validation.
</li>
<li>
*
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/t-digest/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>t-digest:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure used for estimating the percentile of a large dataset without having to store and order all the data points. Used for hardware/software monitoring, online gaming, network traffic monitoring, and predictive maintenance.
</li>
<li>
*
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/top-k/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Top-k:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure for finding the most frequent values in a data stream used for trend discovery.
</li>
<li>
*
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/count-min-sketch/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Count-min sketch:</strong>
</a>
 A probabilistic data structure for estimating how many times a given value appears in a data stream used for sales volume calculations.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/timeseries/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Time series:</strong>
</a>
 Data points indexed in time order used for monitoring sensor data, asset
tracking, and predictive analytics
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Pub/sub</strong>
:
</a>
 A lightweight messaging capability. Publishers send messages to a channel, and subscribers receive messages from that channel.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Stream</strong>
:
</a>
 An append-only log with random access capabilities and complex consumption strategies such as consumer groups. Used for event sourcing, sensor monitoring, and notifications.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/transactions/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Transaction:</strong>
</a>
 Allows the execution of a group of commands in a single step. A request sent by another client will never be served in the middle of the execution of a transaction. This guarantees that the commands are executed as a single isolated operation.
</li>
<li>
<a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/" rel="nofollow">
<strong>Programmability:</strong>
</a>
 Upload and execute Lua scripts on the server. Scripts can employ programmatic control structures and use most of the commands while executing to access the database. Because scripts are executed on the server, reading and writing data from scripts is very efficient.
</li>
</ul>

<p dir="auto">
This section refers to building Redis from source. If you want to get up and running with Redis quickly without needing to build from source see the 
<a href="#getting-started">Getting started section</a>
.
</p>
<p dir="auto">
<strong>These instructions apply to Redis 8.10 and above.</strong>
 For versions lower than 8.10, see the 
<a href="https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#build-redis-from-source">8.8 build instructions</a>
.

<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">
<strong>Configuration files</strong>
: the build steps below tell you to run

<code>./src/redis-server redis.conf</code>
. Release tarballs bake the bundled modules'

<code>loadmodule</code>
 lines and per-module settings directly into 
<code>redis.conf</code>
 during
packaging, so an extracted release tarball is ready to run as-is. When
building from a git checkout instead, that module config lives in the
auto-generated 
<code>redis-full.conf</code>
 produced by 
<code>make modules-update</code>
 (and
regenerated by 
<code>make sync-redis-conf</code>
) — run 
<code>./src/redis-server redis-full.conf</code>
 there. Edit Redis-core settings in

<a href="/redis/redis/blob/unstable/redis.conf">
<code>redis.conf</code>
</a>
. See 
<a href="/redis/redis/blob/unstable/modules/MODULES.md">modules/MODULES.md</a>

for the full config flow.
</p>
</blockquote>

<p dir="auto">
Building Redis with all data structures (JSON, time series, Bloom / cuckoo / count-min / top-k, t-digest, and the Query Engine) needs a build toolchain plus a few version-sensitive dependencies — GCC/Clang, 
<strong>LLVM 21</strong>
, 
<strong>CMake 3.25–3.31.6</strong>
, 
<strong>Rust 1.94</strong>
, OpenSSL, Python 3, and assorted 
<code>-dev</code>
 libraries. Instead of a per-OS package list, the repo installs them for you with 
<strong>
<code>make bootstrap</code>
</strong>
, which detects your OS and installs each bundled module's prerequisites.
</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">
<strong>CMake version range matters.</strong>
 The modules require 
<strong>3.25 ≤ CMake ≤ 3.31.6</strong>
 — CMake 4.x is 
<em>not</em>
 supported and the build will fail with it. On distros that ship CMake 4.x by default (e.g. Ubuntu 26.04), pin a supported version, e.g. 
<code>pip3 install 'cmake==3.31.6'</code>
. Note 
<code>make bootstrap</code>
 only installs CMake when it's missing or too old; it won't downgrade a pre-installed 4.x, so remove/pin that yourself.
</p>
</blockquote>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

<p dir="auto">Pick whichever option fits your environment:</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto">
<strong>Build inside the Docker build environment — recommended.</strong>

The repo ships 
<a href="/redis/redis/blob/unstable/docker/Dockerfile.noble">
<code>docker/Dockerfile.noble</code>
</a>
 (Ubuntu 24.04) with every prerequisite baked in, so you build inside the container and never touch your host toolchain:
</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto">
<pre>docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble 
<span class="pl-c1">.</span>

<span class="pl-c">
<span class="pl-c">#</span>
 Multi-arch (requires `docker buildx` configured):
</span>

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble 
<span class="pl-c1">.</span>

<span class="pl-c">
<span class="pl-c">#</span>
 Build with the working tree mounted:
</span>

docker run --rm -it -v 
<span class="pl-s">
<span class="pl-pds">"</span>
<span class="pl-smi">$PWD</span>
<span class="pl-pds">"</span>
</span>
:/workspace -w /workspace redis-build:noble \
    bash -lc 
<span class="pl-s">
<span class="pl-pds">'</span>
make -j"$(nproc)" && make run
<span class="pl-pds">'</span>
</span>
</pre>

<p dir="auto">
The commands are printed 
<strong>per module</strong>
, so a dependency shared by several
modules appears once for each. Work through them iteratively:
</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>
Copy-paste the commands for a module to install its dependencies.
</li>
<li>
Re-run 
<code>make bootstrap dry-run</code>
 — the deps you just installed no longer
show, so you now see only what's still missing for the remaining modules.
</li>
<li>
Repeat until 
<code>make bootstrap dry-run</code>
 prints no install commands.
</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ol>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">
<strong>Manual, per-OS install</strong>
 (no Docker, and you'd rather not let 
<code>make bootstrap</code>
 touch your host): follow the per-OS dependency instructions in the 8.8 README, which still lists them explicitly — 
<a href="https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#readme">https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#readme</a>
.
</p>
</blockquote>

<p dir="auto">Redis can be compiled and used on Linux, OSX, OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD.
We support big endian and little endian architectures, and both 32 bit and 64-bit systems.</p>
<p dir="auto">
It may compile on Solaris derived systems (for instance SmartOS) but our support for this platform is 
<em>best effort</em>
 and Redis is not guaranteed to work as well as on Linux, OSX, and *BSD.
</p>
<p dir="auto">
To build Redis with all the data structures (including JSON, time series, Bloom filter, cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k, and t-digest) and with Redis Query Engine, make sure first that all the prerequisites are installed (see 
<a href="#install-dependencies-and-build">Install dependencies and build</a>
 above), then clone the bundled modules once and build:
</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto">
<pre>make modules-update
make</pre>

<p dir="auto">
Redis has some dependencies which are included in the 
<code>deps</code>
 directory. 
<code>make</code>
 does not automatically rebuild dependencies even if something in the source code of dependencies changes.
</p>
<p dir="auto">
When you update the source code with 
<code>git pull</code>
 or when code inside the dependencies tree is modified in any other way, make sure to use the following command in order to really clean everything and rebuild from scratch:
</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto">
<pre>make distclean</pre>

<p dir="auto">
If after building Redis with a 32 bit target you need to rebuild it
with a 64 bit target, or the other way around, you need to perform a 
<code>make distclean</code>
 in the root directory of the Redis distribution.
</p>
<p dir="auto">In case of build errors when trying to build a 32 bit binary of Redis, try the following steps:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>

</li>
<li>

<code>make 32bit</code>
:

<code>make CFLAGS="-m32 -march=native" LDFLAGS="-m32"</code>
</li>
</ul>

<p dir="auto">

<code>MALLOC</code>

</p>
<p dir="auto">To force compiling against libc malloc, use:</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto">
<pre>make MALLOC=libc</pre>

<h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Monotonic clock</h3>
<a id="user-content-monotonic-clock" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Monotonic clock" href="#monotonic-clock">
<svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true">
<path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path>
</svg>
</a>
</div>
<p dir="auto">
By default, Redis will build using the POSIX clock_gettime function as the monotonic clock source. On most modern systems, the internal processor clock can be used to improve performance. Cautions can be found here: 
<a href="http://oliveryang.net/2015/09/pitfalls-of-TSC-usage/" rel="nofollow">http://oliveryang.net/2015/09/pitfalls-of-TSC-usage/</a>
</p>
<p dir="auto">
On ARM aarch64 systems, the hardware clock is enabled by default because the ARM Generic Timer is architecturally guaranteed to be available and monotonic on all ARMv8-A processors (see the 
<em>“The Generic Timer in AArch64 state”</em>
 section of the 
<em>Arm Architecture Reference Manual for Armv8-A</em>
).
</p>
<p dir="auto">To build with support for the processor's internal instruction clock on other architectures, use:</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto">
<pre>make CFLAGS=
<span class="pl-s">
<span class="pl-pds">"</span>
-DUSE_PROCESSOR_CLOCK
<span class="pl-pds">"</span>
</span>
</pre>

<p dir="auto">
<strong>License Disclaimer</strong>

If you are using Redis Open Source under AGPLv3 or SSPLv1, you cannot use it together with the Intel Optimizations (Leanvec and LVQ binaries). The reason is that the Intel SVS license is not compatible with those licenses.
The Leanvec and LVQ techniques are closed source and are only available for use with Redis Open Source when distributed under the RSALv2 license.
For more details, please refer to the information provided by Intel 
<a href="https://github.com/intel/ScalableVectorSearch">here</a>
.
</p>
<p dir="auto">By default, Redis with the Redis Query Engine supports SVS-VAMANA index with global 8-bit quantisation. To compile Redis with the Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations, LeanVec and LVQ, use the following:</p>

<pre>make BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes</pre>
